title: Section 1
content:
===============================
echo -e "\n hello"
• -e allows escape characters
===============================
stat [file|directory] 
•  Shows stats, used to check hard link and Access, Modify, Change(AMC),  and blocks(blocks are multiples of 8, when size reaches over 4096 block, the block will show 16)
===============================
cd [file|directory]
• Change directory, shell built in
===============================
xxd [file]
• Hexdump
• Shows 3 cols(aka hexdump); memory, hexadecimal and human readable ascii, those 3 columns combined is called hexdump
xxd -r [file]
• reverse the hexdump to regular ascii and can be used with > to redirect output
===============================
pwd
• print working directory
===============================
ls -lahi -AFC
•  a for all, l for list detail, h for human readable size, A for almost all but doesnt include . and .. , i for inodes, F for type tailing, C is used only for redirecting to files for horizontal format
ls -a --sort name
===============================
Basic regex to know
ls|cp|rm test?.txt [a-z].txt test[0-9].txt *.log
• ? Any character, * any count of char, ~ for $HOME
===============================
cat -nAs [file]
• n for line number, A for showing all including non printing characters, s for squeezing \n
cat > [file]
• > to overwrite and >> to append.      ctrl + d to save and exit, 
===============================
<< (Heredoc)
cat <<EOF > [file]
Name: someone
EOF
• Uhhh EOF can be replaced with anything
===============================
less [file]
• pager, to read in page, can be piped to it to read in page too
===============================
head -n 5 [file]
• n for line count , top 5 lines in this case
===============================
tail -f [file]
tail -n +1 ./*
• f for live following the last message like logs, n for line count, -n +1 is used for mentioning the file names when printing multiple files
===============================
grep -rivn -A 2 -B 2 "search_word" [file|dir]
• r for recursive search used with directory, i for ignore case, v for invert, n for line number, A & B for including line after and before
grep -C 3 -E "=+" data.gxt
• C for including lines both before and after, E for expression, "=+" matches =, ===, or more, 
• "={2,}\s+\w+" 2 or more times of =, \s+ 1 or more spaces, \w+ 1 or more words
===============================
find . -name "logs" -type d
• type d for directory, f for file
find / -iname "*.log" -type f -user username -group groupname -size 33c -exec rm {} \;
• -iname for case insensitive search, size c for bytes, +10M for more than 10 Megabytes, -1G for less than 1 Gigabyte
• exec for execute on what it founds, {} placeholder, \; terminates cmd
===============================
locate [file|dir]
• unlike find which crawls in hard drive storage, it searchs in /var/lib/mlocate/mlocate.db to locate extremely fast
• Do "sudo updatedb" to renew db if new files aren't found
===============================
which -a [cmd]
• a for search all. It searches the cmd listed in $PATH and shows the first found executable script with that name, because, by default if you execute a cmd it goes through $PATH from left to right. in short, it shows the path of cmd
===============================
type -ta [cmd|/path/to/cmd]
• a for all including alias, t for printing only type(alias, shellbuiltin) used for shell scripting, a for all 
===============================
whereis -l [cmd]
• Just like which cmd, ignores $PATH, ignore symlinks to not get duplicate result, useful if $PATH is broken incase malicious users or anything, also used for getting man page's location
• l for listing the hardcoded path whereis uses to search for, man: means it searches man pages in there
===============================
whatis [cmd]
• One line explaining what the cmd does
===============================
string [file]
• Extracts human readable texts (4 or more printable characters)
===============================
man [cmd]
• manual page
info [cmd]
• more detailed then man with eg., but not all cmds support
===============================
apropos "search text"
• searches man pages, output will look like grep, egrep and other cmds
===============================
--help --version(sometimes support -v)
• Most cmds have these options written in it
===============================
ln -s [target] [path/link name]
• Soft link and hard link, -s for soft link
===============================
readlink -f [link]
• shows where the link points to, f for follow link to the end and shows absolute path, yes f follows links
===============================
file [file]
• Used to check the type of file like ascii text(your everyday normal text) or tar archived or zip with algorithm(gzip)
===============================
Archiving(tar,..) & Compressing(gzip)
--------------------------------------------
tar -czvf [archive.tar.gz] [folder|file to tar]
tar -cjvf [archive.tar.bz2] [path/to tar]
tar -cJvf [archive.tar.xz] [specify what to tar]
tar -xvf [archive.tar.gz]
tar -tf or -tvf to view contents inside
• c for archive, z for gzip(tar uses gzip), v for verbose, f for specifying file,  j for bzip2, J for Xz, no zip for just archive, if the "file" cmd says its archived its probably tar
• x for extract and modern linux automatically knows which type of zip to extract, itll unarchive and if its compressed, itll extract in one go
===============================
zip -r myfiles.zip /path/to/folder
unzip myfiles.zip
• Unlike tar, zip combines archiving and compression , is cross platform tool, so best use for using between Windows and Linux or such
• r for recursive for dir, -e for encryption
===============================
gzip -k app.log
gunzip app.log.gz
• k for keep original and use copy
===============================
bzip2 -k app.txt
bunzip2 app.txt.bz2
• k for keep original same as gzip
===============================
touch [file|/path/to/file]
===============================
mkdir -p dir1 dir2 /path/to/dir "my dir"
• p creates path even if didnt exist
===============================
rm -rf file1.txt dir2
rmdir empty_dir
• r for recrusive, f for force, rmdir only works for empty dir,
===============================
cp source.txt path/renamed_dest.txt
cp -r docs/ source1.txt source2.txt dest/
• r for recursive
===============================
mv -iv [src(s)(file | dir)] [dest (file | dir)]
• If dest doesnt exist it renames, -v for verbose, -i for confirmation incase overwrite, doesnt need -r
===============================
tee (99% used with pipe)
echo "error: crash" | tee -a failure.log | grep "error"
echo "10.0.0.5 prod" | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts 
• tee pipes things. If no pipe at end to catch the stdout, then it will show in your terminal, -a is for appending.
• often used for sudo tee because echo "write" >, the > doesnt have sudo perm
===============================

===============================
|| 0 = stdin | 1 = stdout | 2 = stderr ||
> = 1>
find /etc -name "*.conf" 2>/dev/null
• 2> redirect error, no space after 2>

cron_job.sh &> deployment.log
• &> redirect success and error
===============================
cut -d ':' -f 1 /etc/passwd
• delimiter, fields
===============================
sort -nrh names.txt
• Numeric sort, reverse, human numeric(2K, 4M, 1G)
===============================
uniq -cd names.txt
• Count, duplicates only, always with sort
===============================
tr (cannot use directly, must be piped|)
echo "devops engineering" | tr 'a-z' 'A-Z'
echo "DevOps     and     DevSecOps" | tr -s ' '
• '[:lower:]' '[:upper:]' '[:alpha:]' '[:digit:]' '0-9' '[:punct]' '[:space:]'
• -d for delete, -s for squeeze
===============================
wc -lwc -mL [file]
• line count, word count, byte cout
• -m character count, -L count of characters in the longest line
• docker ps -q | wc -l
===============================
nl -n ln -v 1 [file|or redirected|]
• -n ln for spacing , -n nl, -v starting no.
===============================
xargs -I {}
• -I {} placeholder
find . -name "*.log" | xargs -I {} mv {} /var/log/backup/
ls *.sh | xargs -I {} ln -s {} /usr/local/bin/{}
echo "a b c" | xargs -n1 -I {} touch {}.txt
find . -name "*.tmp" | xargs rm -f
• Normal xargs attaches the output to the end {} can help in middle, -n1 uses one argument as a one line of cmd, -n2 and so on, whitespaces and newlines are its default delimiter
===============================
join -t ',' file1.csv file2.csv
join -1 2 -2 1 file1.csv file3.csv
• Merges first column of matchings, -t for defining delimiter
• -1 for first file's column's number
===============================
echo "http://api.local" | sed 's/http/https/g'
sed '/kube-system/d' cluster.log
• s/ replace,  /g global, /d is delete
• -E extended regex, allows advanced regex
===============================
